title: Judo: groundwork, breakfalls, scoring, and Kano's principles
note: Katame-waza covers pins, strangles, and joint locks; in IJF contests joint locks are applied only to the elbow. Ukemi, breakfalling, makes full-force throwing safe. Ippon ends a contest; below it come waza-ari and, since 2025, yuko again. Kano's two principles are seiryoku zen'yo and jita kyoei.

read.title: Efficiency and mutual welfare
text: Jigoro Kano wanted judo to be more than a way to win fights. He summed up its core in two phrases. Seiryoku zen'yo means the most efficient use of physical and mental energy: break balance first, use the opponent's movement, and spend no more effort than a task requires. Kano presented it as a principle not only of throwing but of daily life.

Jita kyoei means mutual welfare and benefit. Training partners help each other improve, and that cooperation should carry over into society. In practice it shows up in small habits: a thrower controls the fall, a partner who taps is released at once, and every session begins and ends with a bow.

Ukemi makes this possible. Because judoka learn to fall forward, backward, and to the side, slapping the mat to spread the impact and tucking the chin to protect the head, they can be thrown hard thousands of times. Randori, free practice against a resisting partner, then tests technique for real without breaking the partnership.
Contests keep the same ideals. A clean throw with control or a 20-second pin earns ippon and ends the match.
